extracted.intended_audience: aspiring MFA students, current MFA students (especially writers of color), writing program faculty/administrators, and organizers of writing workshops for POC
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the inclusiveness and supportiveness of creative-writing MFA workshops—especially how they serve (or fail) writers of color—and designing/choosing workshops that center POC experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty and student diversity ('too white')
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should not be overwhelmingly white in faculty or student body; presence of faculty of color in the fiction program matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junot Díaz labels his MFA experience 'too white' and explains that Cornell had almost no people of color and 'no faculty of color in the fiction program.' The text emphasizes that lack of faculty of color signals institutional indifference and shapes what is read, taught, and defended in workshop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop worldview must acknowledge race as a social force
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops should recognize racial identity and racism as real, relevant forces that impact writers and their work, rather than treating race as irrelevant or secondary (e.g., 'it's class!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticizes workshops that operate under a 'white straight male default' and an 'almost lunatical belief that race was no longer a major social force.' Such denial results in silence about race and eliminates instruction or discussion about how racial identities impact writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum/readings must include writers and traditions of color
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading lists and taught traditions should include writers of color (e.g., Toni Morrison, Cherríe Moraga, Edwidge Danticat, Alice Walker, Jamaica Kincaid) rather than only white writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Díaz contrasts the program's exclusive education in writers like William Gaddis and Alice Munro with the absence of writers of color; he implies that exposure to diverse literary traditions is essential to a workshop that truly serves POC students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty should actively intervene against racist peer behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Professors must correct or challenge classmates' racist assumptions and edits, not ignore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He recounts a peer who erased 'big' words from a Latino writer's story claiming 'that's not the way Spanish people talk' and notes the professor 'never corrected or even questioned said peer.' The lack of faculty response is criticized as tacit acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshops must allow discussion of racial identity and its impact on craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops should provide space and instruction to explore racial identities, how those identities shape perspective, and how they affect choices in craft and subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Díaz stresses that in his workshop 'we never explored our racial identities or how they impacted our writing—at all,' and that attempts to raise such issues were sometimes shut down as 'politicizing the Pure Art.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Program culture should not treat race discussions as 'political correctness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious workshops should not dismiss conversations about race as irrelevant to literary craft or as mere 'political correctness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He gives examples of peers and faculty saying 'Our workshop is about writing, not political correctness,' using that position to silence race-related critique; the rubric implies this attitude is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center contributions of writers of color as core to Literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops should privilege the experiences and contributions of POC as central to literature, not as adjunct or marginal subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Díaz describes the aim of VONA as making POC contributions 'privileged rather than marginalized; encouraged rather than ignored; discussed intelligently rather than trivialized,' arguing that POC work should be considered core to 'Literature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide safe, supportive community and mutual witnessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should cultivate solidarity, support networks, and spaces where writers of color 'see' one another and serve as witnesses for each other's work and struggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author credits a campus Latino student movement and later VONA with creating the solidarity that 'saved' him; he emphasizes that such community made workshop bearable and fostered both personal survival and artistic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and wellbeing of writers of color as an evaluative metric
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy program should retain and nurture POC students rather than driving them out; frequent departures of POC students indicate systemic failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Díaz recounts losing talented peers—most notably 'Athena,' who quit and never published—arguing that the loss of writers of color ('lost time, lost opportunities, lost people') is a measure of workshop harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional accountability: hiring faculty of color matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Active hiring of faculty of color is a concrete step programs must take; bringing in such faculty changes curriculum and workshop dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He highlights the successful hiring of Helena María Viramontes as a crowning triumph of student organizing and an example of how a faculty of color can create workshops where 'race existed and was not an interloper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of alternative/dedicated workshops for POC
rubrics_metrics.description: Where mainstream programs fail, dedicated workshops for writers of color (e.g., VONA) provide a necessary antidote and model for practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Díaz describes founding the Voices of Our Nation Workshop as an attempt to create a 'safe supportive environment' where POC experiences are centered and where craft, critique, and community can flourish; he positions these spaces as remedies to the 'oppressive biases of mainstream workshops.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage intra-POC dialogue and collective care
rubrics_metrics.description: POC writers in programs should be encouraged to talk across differences, support one another, and act collectively rather than retreating into isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He laments that 'we Calibans had all retreated into our separate bolt holes' rather than forming interventions for peers like Athena; the essay suggests that mutual accountability and care among POC could improve retention and creative output.
